clinicalPearls: Microsporidia are spore-forming, obligate intracellular organisms now classified with the fungi, transmitted by ingesting or inhaling environmentally resistant spores
Enterocytozoon bieneusi and Encephalitozoon intestinalis are the commonest species causing chronic, watery, non-bloody diarrhoea and wasting in people with advanced HIV
The infection came to prominence as an AIDS-defining cause of intractable diarrhoea before widespread antiretroviral therapy
Encephalitozoon species can disseminate beyond the gut to cause keratoconjunctivitis, sinusitis, hepatitis, nephritis and encephalitis, unlike the largely enteric E. bieneusi

Diagnosis relies on detecting the small spores in stool or biopsy using chromotrope-based (modified trichrome) stains that colour the spores pinkish-red against a pale background, or with calcofluor and immunofluorescence
Albendazole is effective against Encephalitozoon species, whereas E. bieneusi responds poorly and is better managed with fumagillin where available
Immune reconstitution with antiretroviral therapy is the most important measure for durable resolution in HIV-associated disease
reference.pathophysiology: Microsporidia are unicellular, obligate intracellular organisms that infect host cells by explosively everting a coiled polar tubule, through which the sporoplasm is injected into the cytoplasm. Intracellular multiplication culminates in the release of resistant spores that are shed in stool, urine or respiratory secretions and transmit infection. In the gut, infection of enterocytes causes villous atrophy, epithelial disarray and malabsorption with a secretory diarrhoea. Effective control depends on cell-mediated immunity, so heavy chronic infection and dissemination to eye, sinuses, liver, kidney and central nervous system occur predominantly in profound immunosuppression such as advanced HIV.
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy with chromotrope (modified trichrome) staining for spores
Calcofluor white or immunofluorescent staining of faecal smears
Small-bowel biopsy with electron microscopy when stool testing is inconclusive
Urine, corneal scrapings or other specimens when dissemination is suspected
redFlags: Chronic dehydrating diarrhoea with severe wasting in advanced HIV
Features of disseminated disease such as renal, hepatic or neurological involvement
Failure of enteric symptoms to settle despite species-directed therapy
reference.prognosis: In immunocompetent hosts infection is usually mild and self-limiting; in advanced HIV it can be chronic and disabling, though outcomes improved markedly with immune reconstitution and species-directed therapy.
pitfalls: Missing the tiny spores because routine stool microscopy lacks a chromotrope or fluorescent stain
Treating all species with albendazole and expecting response, when Enterocytozoon bieneusi responds poorly
Overlooking extraintestinal sites such as the eye in disseminated Encephalitozoon infection
Neglecting antiretroviral therapy, without which relapse is likely
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat Encephalitozoon species with albendazole, and Enterocytozoon bieneusi with fumagillin where available
Restore cell-mediated immunity with antiretroviral therapy in HIV, which is central to clearing and preventing relapse of infection
Provide supportive care with rehydration, electrolyte correction, nutritional support and antidiarrhoeal agents for the secretory diarrhoea
Treat microsporidial keratoconjunctivitis with topical fumagillin alongside systemic therapy
Monitor the CD4 count and clinical response, remaining alert to dissemination to eye, sinuses, liver, kidney and central nervous system
Advise on prevention through safe water and hand hygiene, particularly in the immunocompromised
